title: The Distant Undertow
premise: Silas Pemberton, a night librarian who has spent twelve years guarding a family secret about the death of their younger brother, is unmasked at their father's funeral by a stranger who calls the family by their true surname, Vane. The stranger, a journalist named Ada Okonkwo, holds letters proving the brother's death was no accident and that Silas's uncle, now a powerful judge, orchestrated both the cover-up and Silas's lifelong silence. As the old neighborhood faces demolition and rerouting, Silas must return to the drowned mill district where it happened, recover the buried evidence, and choose between the safety of invisibility and testifying outside any court that would have them. The novel ends with Silas reading the truth aloud at a public hearing as the last bus to the old neighborhood makes its final run—justice delivered not by law but by witness.
about_author: Paloma Marchetti worked for nine years as an archivist in a coastal municipal library before turning to fiction full-time. Her writing explores quiet people caught in loud inheritances, and she lives above a defunct ferry terminal with her dog, Bricole.

chapters.title: The Hours Nobody Claims
chapters.summary: Third-person limited on Silas, shelving returns in the dead hours of the Halcyon Branch Library while the city outside never quite sleeps. We learn of the ritual of 'almost saying it'—the sentence Silas has rehearsed for twelve years and never finished. Emotional beat: loneliness mistaken for peace.

chapters.title: A Funeral in Full Light
chapters.summary: Silas attends their father's funeral, performing grief at a distance they've perfected. POV shifts briefly to cousin Marisol, who notices Silas counting exits. The chapter establishes the family's polished public face. Emotional beat: the exhaustion of being a stranger among your own blood.

chapters.title: The Name Nobody Uses
chapters.summary: At the reception, a woman—Ada Okonkwo—addresses Silas as 'Vane,' a surname retired decades ago. She leaves a card and one line: 'I know what happened at the mill.' Silas burns nothing but cannot sleep. Emotional beat: the floor giving way beneath a carefully built life.

chapters.title: Twelve Years of Almost
chapters.summary: Flashback chapter in Silas's first-person voice: the night their brother Theo died in the flooded mill district, the uncle's arrival before the police, the papers signed, the name changed. Emotional beat: guilt compounding into identity—Silas became silence itself.

chapters.title: Ada Okonkwo, Asking
chapters.summary: Ada visits the library at closing time, laying out photocopied letters between Uncle Ambrose Vane and a former site foreman. She doesn't threaten; she simply refuses to leave until Silas looks. POV: alternating close-third. Emotional beat: the terror and relief of being seen.

chapters.title: What the Judge Built
chapters.summary: Silas researches Ambrose's rise from mill owner's son to appellate judge, discovering the neighborhood's demolition schedule conveniently timed after his father's death. Marisol warns Silas that Ambrose protects the family 'whether we ask or not.' Emotional beat: dawning understanding of how deep the corruption runs.

chapters.title: The Rerouting Notice
chapters.summary: City notices announce the last bus route through the old neighborhood will be discontinued in six weeks—the same corridor that passes the mill. Silas realizes the physical door to the past is closing on a deadline. Emotional beat: urgency disguised as civic paperwork.

chapters.title: Marisol's Bargain
chapters.summary: Marisol confesses she was paid annually to keep her own memory vague—a hush stipend dressed as inheritance. Her POV chapter reveals she loved Theo too. She gives Silas the key to the family boathouse. Emotional beat: two silences recognizing each other.

chapters.title: Letters in the Boathouse Wall
chapters.summary: Behind rotted paneling, Silas finds Theo's own letters—written weeks before his death, describing foremen moving crates at night and threatening to report it. POV: Silas, hands shaking over water-stained paper. Emotional beat: the dead brother suddenly louder than the living judge.

chapters.title: Ambrose at the Door
chapters.summary: Uncle Ambrose appears at Silas's apartment, courteous and glacial, offering a promotion, a transfer, a clean erasure. He mentions Ada's name unprompted. Silas says almost—it again—and he leaves satisfied. Emotional beat: the seduction of safety, and its cost made visible.

chapters.title: The Foreman's Daughter
chapters.summary: Silas tracks down Ruth Ellery, daughter of the foreman named in Theo's letters, now a hospice nurse. She confirms her father confessed on his deathbed. She agrees to speak—but only if Silas speaks first. Emotional beat: solidarity forged between people the family used.

chapters.title: Night Shift Testimony
chapters.summary: Ada drafts the story; Silas fact-checks their own childhood against archives, finding the fire report altered. A break-in at the library shakes them—someone searched the local history room. Emotional beat: paranoia tightening, resolve hardening.

chapters.title: What Invisibility Costs
chapters.summary: A quiet middle-chapter: Silas walks the old neighborhood at dusk, cataloguing what demolition will erase—the corner store, the schoolyard, the mill's skeleton. They realize staying invisible meant letting Theo stay invisible too. Emotional beat: mourning converted into purpose.

chapters.title: The Leak
chapters.summary: Ada's editor kills the story under legal pressure; a rival outlet runs a smear piece painting Silas as unstable. Colleagues look at Silas differently. Marisol goes silent. Emotional beat: the machinery of power grinding down the small people who resist it.

chapters.title: Ruth's Condition
chapters.summary: Ruth reveals her father kept the original crate manifests hidden inside a memorial bench near the mill—his penance. But the benches are scheduled for removal within days. POV alternates Ruth/Silas. Emotional beat: hope on a countdown clock.

chapters.title: Last Bus North
chapters.summary: Silas rides the final scheduled bus along the old route, sitting where Theo used to sit, watching the neighborhood pass like a slideshow of everything unsaid. They get off at the mill stop, which will never be a stop again. Emotional beat: pilgrimage, farewell, and arrival all at once.

chapters.title: The Bench at Low Tide
chapters.summary: In fog, Silas pries open the memorial bench and retrieves the manifests—shipping records proving Ambrose moved contraband through the mill and killed Theo for knowing. Ambrose arrives, having followed them. Confrontation without violence: he offers everything one last time. Emotional beat: the moment almost becomes never.

chapters.title: Almost, No Longer
chapters.summary: Cornered at the mill's edge with Ambrose blocking the path, Silas finally finishes the twelve-year sentence aloud: 'You killed my brother, and I helped you hide it.' Ambrose's composure cracks. Silas records it. Emotional beat: catharsis—the sentence completed at last.

chapters.title: The Hearing
chapters.summary: At the city's public comment session on the redevelopment, Silas takes the microphone and reads Theo's letters, the manifests' contents, and their own confession of complicity. Ruth stands beside them; Marisol arrives late and stands too. Emotional beat: justice performed in the only court that would hold them—witness.

chapters.title: Consequences, Unevenly Distributed
chapters.summary: Ambrose resigns quietly; prosecutors open a file that may go nowhere. The law moves slowly and imperfectly, but the record exists now, permanent and public. Ada publishes. Silas keeps their job. Emotional beat: justice outside the law—imperfect, insufficient, real.

chapters.title: What the Neighborhood Remembers
chapters.summary: Demolition begins anyway, but residents hold a remembrance walk along the dead bus route, telling stories aloud—including, finally, Theo's. Silas walks it with Marisol and Ruth. Emotional beat: collective memory as the truest inheritance.

chapters.title: The Distant Undertow
chapters.summary: Months later, Silas closes the library at dawn and pins Theo's photograph above the returns desk, finishing the ritual differently now: saying things fully, out loud, to patrons and strangers alike. The undertow still pulls, but Silas swims with it rather than against. Final beat: a life rebuilt around truth instead of silence.
